lesson.title: Teaching cyber safety across the school
lesson.subtitle: Little and often, in every subject

video.title: Teaching cyber safety across the school
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher and the school's cyber lead (main character)
Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher (opens the lesson)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor in the school hall after an assembly, pupils filing out happily. Then a month later: a pupil's phone screen with a chat bubble from a 'game moderator' and a code being sent.
scenes.animation: Hall fades to a calendar flipping one month; the phone buzzes.
scenes.narration: Every year, we held one cyber safety assembly. The pupils loved it. A month later, one of them sent her one-time code to a stranger pretending to be a game moderator.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Teaching cyber safety across the school
scenes.narration: Today: how to teach cyber safety little and often, across subjects and year groups.

scenes.visual: Two columns: on one side a single big assembly fading away; on the other, many small coloured blocks across a school year that build into a wall.
scenes.animation: The big block fades; small blocks stack up term by term.
scenes.narration: One talk a year is forgotten. Short activities, every term, in many subjects, become habits. Ten minutes in maths, ten in languages, ten in science: it adds up, and nobody needs a whole new lesson.

scenes.visual: Five subject doors along a school corridor, each opening on a small cyber activity: a cipher wheel, a scam message, a network diagram, a law book, a poster.
scenes.animation: Doors open one after another as each subject is named.
scenes.narration: Maths can count password combinations, or crack a secret code. Languages can study the wording of a scam. Science can show how messages travel across a network. Social studies can talk about rights and laws, and art can design the posters.

scenes.visual: Two pupils of different ages side by side: a younger pupil with three simple cards, an older pupil with a phone showing settings.
scenes.animation: Cards fan out for each pupil in turn.
scenes.narration: Match the message to the age. Younger pupils learn three things: keep private things private, ask an adult, and be kind. Older pupils add privacy settings, two-step sign-in, scams and their digital footprint.

scenes.visual: A road crossing near the school: a small child holding an adult's hand, then an older pupil crossing a bigger road alone, looking both ways.
scenes.animation: The scene pans from the small road to the big one.
scenes.narration: It’s like road safety. We don’t teach it once to five-year-olds and stop; we repeat it, with more detail, as children start crossing bigger roads alone.

scenes.visual: Salma at the staffroom table with three plan cards. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Character slides in; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Which plan will really change what our pupils do online?

scenes.visual: The 'short activities' card gets a blue check badge. Small blocks in different subject colours stack into a wall labelled 'habits'.
scenes.narration: Short activities, in many subjects, every term. Pupils meet the same idea in different places and practise it, and that is what turns knowing into doing.

scenes.visual: A quiet corner of a classroom. A teacher sits at the pupil's level, listening, notebook closed. Then the teacher walks to an office door marked with a shield.
scenes.animation: Steps appear one by one beside the scene.
scenes.narration: Sometimes a pupil will tell you about bullying, threats, or someone asking for photos. Listen calmly, believe them, and don’t blame. Never ask to see or forward images, but ask them to keep the messages. Tell your safeguarding lead the same day, and if anyone is demanding money or more images, the answer is never to pay.

scenes.visual: A parent at home reads a short tip in the official parents' group on their phone, then helps their child set a screen lock.
scenes.animation: The tip slides in; the phone shows a lock.
scenes.narration: Parents are part of the plan. Share one short tip a month in the official parents’ group: how to set a screen lock, what a scam looks like, why codes are never shared. Keep it short and kind, in the languages families speak.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor, serious and calm. Two answer cards bounce in: a phone with an arrow (send it to me) and an open hand beside a shield (listen and report).
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A pupil tells you someone online is threatening to share a photo of her unless she pays. Should you ask her to send you the photo, as evidence?

scenes.visual: The 'listen and report' card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: No: never ask for or forward images; listen, and tell your safeguarding lead the same day. Remember: little and often, in every subject, matched to age, with parents in the loop.

scenes.visual: Salma's maths class: pupils in pairs swap folded notes of letters, counting letters on scrap paper and grinning when one cracks the code.
scenes.animation: Notes swap hands; a letter tally grows; a pupil raises a hand in triumph.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: ten minutes of secret codes. Pupils hide a short message by shifting each letter and swap with a partner to decode it, then crack a longer one by counting letters.

checkpoints.prompt: Which plan is most likely to change what pupils do online?

options.text: One long assembly at the start of the year
Short activities in many subjects, every term
A poster on the computer room wall

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: short practice, repeated in different subjects, turns knowledge into habits.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: an assembly is forgotten and a poster becomes wallpaper. Short activities, repeated in many subjects, build habits.

checkpoints.prompt: A pupil tells you someone online is threatening to share a photo of her unless she pays. Should you ask her to send you the photo, as evidence?

options.text: No: I listen, and tell the safeguarding lead today

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: never ask for or forward images. Listen, reassure her, and pass it to the safeguarding lead the same day.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: asking for the image spreads it further and can break the law. Listen, don’t blame, and tell the safeguarding lead the same day.
